prompt: Please review the proposed DynamoDB data model in docs/design/orders-table-design.md and the supporting files in this project. I own the Orders migration and need a go/no-go view before the March development cutover. The design is meant to keep the API stable while moving persistence, reporting, and fulfillment reads onto one table. I am especially concerned about whether the stated traffic, limits, costs, and existing service behavior line up in production, and whether the migration handles the less common cases that the examples may hide. Write the review to REVIEW.md at the top of the project. Explain the concrete consequence of each important issue and give a developer-actionable fix. End the review with one fenced json list of findings, each with location (the section number of the document, like 3.2), severity (critical, high, medium, low or nit), issue, and fix.

checks.cmd: node -e 'const fs=require("fs");const t=fs.readFileSync("REVIEW.md","utf8");let L=null;for(const m of t.matchAll(/^\x60\x60\x60([a-z]*)[ \t]*\n([\s\S]*?)^\x60\x60\x60[ \t]*$/gim)){if(m[1]&&m[1].toLowerCase()!=="json")continue;let d;try{d=JSON.parse(m[2])}catch{continue}const l=Array.isArray(d)?d:Array.isArray(d&&d.findings)?d.findings:null;if(l&&l.every(x=>x&&typeof x==="object"&&!Array.isArray(x))){L=l;break}}if(!L||!L.length)process.exit(1);const S=["critical","high","medium","low","nit"];process.exit(L.every(x=>x.location&&S.includes(String(x.severity).toLowerCase())&&(x.issue||x.fix||x.text))?0:1)'

node -e 'const fs=require("fs");const t=fs.readFileSync("REVIEW.md","utf8");let L=null;for(const m of t.matchAll(/^\x60\x60\x60([a-z]*)[ \t]*\n([\s\S]*?)^\x60\x60\x60[ \t]*$/gim)){if(m[1]&&m[1].toLowerCase()!=="json")continue;let d;try{d=JSON.parse(m[2])}catch{continue}const l=Array.isArray(d)?d:Array.isArray(d&&d.findings)?d.findings:null;if(l&&l.every(x=>x&&typeof x==="object"&&!Array.isArray(x))){L=l;break}}if(!L||!L.length)process.exit(1);const H=new Set();for(const l of fs.readFileSync("docs/design/orders-table-design.md","utf8").split("\n")){const m=l.match(/^#+\s*(?:section\s*)?(\d+(?:\.\d+)*)/i);if(m)H.add(m[1])}process.exit(L.every(x=>{const m=String(x.location).match(/\d+(?:\.\d+)*/);return m&&H.has(m[0])})?0:1)'

rubric.criterion: Fail: The review misses most important planted issues or gives unsupported findings and no actionable fixes. Partial: The review identifies some real issues with project-specific consequences and actionable fixes but omits or weakly explains other important risks. Pass: The review identifies each important real issue in this project, explains its concrete consequence using the packet's facts, and gives a developer-actionable fix without inventing problems (code cannot check this because it requires judging technical reasoning and evidence).

findingsKey.finding: Using the UTC order date as the sole partition key concentrates the launch peak on one partition, exceeding the stated per-partition write baseline and making checkout latency vulnerable to a daily hot spot.

Customer history is implemented as a filtered table scan even though the service must support 2,400 requests per second and customers with more than 100,000 orders, so the access pattern has no bounded key-based read.

GSI1 projects every order attribute while the fulfillment path reads only orderId, customerId, and updatedAt, unnecessarily duplicating large line-bearing items and roughly doubling index write and storage cost.
The list representation cannot fit the observed 774 KB order or the planned 1,200-line bulk order within DynamoDB's 400 KB item limit, so valid orders will fail to write or read.

Read-then-write counter updates can lose concurrent increments and count redelivered status events twice, making fulfillment workload counts unreliable despite the event contract requiring idempotency.
Scanning the entire growing table every hour cannot stay within the 400 USD reporting allocation as the table grows from 250 GB toward 1.1 TB, and it does not provide a bounded incremental workload.

items.text: Requires a precise authorization boundary for customer reads and reporting reads, including how the service prevents an authenticated caller from fetching another customer's order by identifier.
items.source: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.text: Asks for a tested recovery procedure with an explicit recovery point objective, restored-index validation, and evidence that the four-hour target holds rather than leaving the test until after cutover.
Calls for a reconciliation and completeness signal for hourly and daily reports so operators can distinguish a late report, partial scan, and valid empty result.
Questions how table names, feature flags, and role bindings are isolated across development, migration, and production environments instead of relying on configuration conventions alone.
Requests a decision record that compares the one-table choice with an export or separate reporting store and records why the rejected options fit the stated constraints less well.
items.source: MADR, Markdown Architectural Decision Records, https://github.com/adr/madr (MIT OR CC0-1.0)

items.text: Asks how the dual-write retry queue is drained and audited before reads switch, including what happens to an order whose PostgreSQL write succeeded but whose DynamoDB write remains unknown.
items.source: RFC 9700, Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700 (IETF Trust Legal Provisions)

weakAnswers: The proposal is clear and the one-table approach looks ready for implementation.
Consider scalability, monitoring, and failure handling before launch.
The key design, indexes, migration stages, and cost estimate are all documented; approve with routine follow-up testing.
Add more detail about future growth and keep an eye on latency.

verdicts.note: Prompt asks for general review of traffic, limits, costs, and service behavior alignment without naming review methods, checklists, or hinting at specific problems.
Clear instructions: review DynamoDB model in docs/design/orders-table-design.md and supporting files, write to REVIEW.md, include section numbers, severity, issue, and fix in JSON list.
Key items require cross-referencing multiple files, understanding DynamoDB constraints, and performing calculations; not findable by quick shallow review.
All key items are supported by evidence in fixture files: traffic forecasts, cost allocations, service limits, and design descriptions.
Fixture provides necessary constraints without explicit pointers; no comments, test names, or file names highlight planted problems.

items.note: The prompt asks to review a design document and write REVIEW.md with findings; it specifies no method/process/framework for how to work and contains no decoy.
The fixture contains the design document with defects but does not state the 6 hidden findings (k1-k6) that the tests check for; the answer is not listed anywhere in fixture.

The hidden key.json findings (k1-k6) all map to concrete sections in the fixture's orders-table-design.md (3.2,3.3,4.1,3.4,3.5,6.3); the rubric's Pass anchor matches by asking to identify each important issue with actionable fixes.

A competent developer could read the design doc and context files, understand traffic targets (1800 writes/s, 2400 reqs/s), item limits (400KB), event contract (idempotency), and reporting budget (400 USD), and identify all 6 defects; the grader accepts variations in wording and structure.
